Maʿārif ul Qurʾān supports this with the hadith reported by **Bukhari and Muslim** from Sayyidnā Muʿawiyah (may Allah be pleased with him), in which the Prophet ﷺ said that a group of his Ummah will always remain on the truth and dominant, unharmed by those who fail to support them and those who defy them, until the Last Hour begins.

Either way, the message to a believer living centuries after revelation is the same: **being late is not being excluded.**

## The night the Prophet ﷺ was shown the nations

Ibn Kathir closes this passage with the narration Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud — and it is the passage's emotional summit.

The Companions were with the Prophet ﷺ one night, and in the morning he told them that some Prophets and their nations had been displayed before him. A Prophet would pass in front of him with a group of men, another with three men, and another **with nobody with him**. (Qatadah, one of the narrators, then recited: "Is there not among you a single right-minded man?" — 11:78.) Until Musa, son of ʿImran, passed him, with a great crowd from the Children of Israel.

"So, I asked my Lord, 'Who is this?' He said, 'This is your brother Musa, son of ʿImran, and those who followed him among the Children of Israel.' I said, 'O Lord! Where is my Ummah?' Allah said, 'Look to your right on the hill' — and I looked and saw faces of men. Allah said, 'Are you pleased?' and I said, 'I am pleased, O Lord!' Allah said, 'Look to the horizon to your left' — and I saw faces of men. He again asked, 'Are you pleased?' and I said, 'I am pleased, O Lord!' He said, 'And with them are seventy thousand who will enter Paradise without reckoning.'"

ʿUkkashah bin Mihsan from Bani Asad, one of those who participated in the battle of Badr, said, "O Allah's Messenger! Invoke Allah to make me one of them." The Prophet ﷺ said, "O Allah, make him one of them." Another man asked the same, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "**ʿUkkashah beat you to it.**"

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Therefore, may I sacrifice my father and mother for you! Try to be among the seventy thousand, or among the crowds on the right, or the crowds that covered the side of the horizon, because I saw large crowds gathering on that side." He ﷺ continued, "I hope that you will be a fourth of the people of Paradise" — and they said *Allahu Akbar*. "I hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise" — *Allahu Akbar*. "I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise" — *Allahu Akbar*. **And then he recited: "A multitude of those will be from the first generation. And a multitude of those will be from the later generations."**

The Companions said to each other, "Who are those seventy thousand?" and supposed they were those who were born in Islam and did not associate anything with Allah in worship. When what they said reached the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Rather, they are the people who do not get treated by cauterization, do not ask for *ruqyah* (getting oneself treated by the recitation of some verses of the Qur'an) and do not draw an evil omen from birds — **but put their trust only in their Lord.**"

Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has many chains of narration, collected in the Ṣaḥīḥs and in other collections of hadith.

## Living it

- **Aim high, and take the next rank if you miss it.** The Prophet's ﷺ own instruction structures the whole passage: be among the seventy thousand; failing that, the crowds on the right; failing that, the crowds of the horizon. The people of the right are lesser in rank than the foremost — and their portion is still everything described in ayat 35–38. Never let the highest station being out of reach become a reason to stop climbing.
- **Trust is the qualifying trait.** When the Companions guessed at the seventy thousand, the Prophet ﷺ redirected them to *tawakkul* — hearts that put their trust only in their Lord, rather than in cauterization, requested *ruqyah*, or omens. That is a matter of the inside, available to anyone.
- **Let ayah 35 change how you look at ageing.** The verse the Prophet ﷺ recited to a weeping old woman is yours too. What this life takes from the body of a believer, Allah answers with a new creation.
- **Take ayah 37 as a standard for now.** *ʿUrub* is love that runs both ways; *atrāb* is being matched, side by side, neither outgrowing the other. That is what Allah calls a reward — which tells you what a marriage in this world is meant to reach toward.

passages.title: The people of the left and their earned torment
passages.tafsir:
This passage turns the surah's camera onto the third and last of its groups: **the People of the Left**. Ayah 41 announces them with a cry of dread, ayat 42–44 describe the place they will be in, and ayat 45–46 tell us — in just two short clauses — exactly what put them there. That is what holds the unit together: **a punishment, and then its cause.** Nothing here is arbitrary. Ibn Kathir's own heading over these lines is "Those on the Left and Their Recompense," and after describing their state he says plainly that Allah then "stated that they deserve this end."

## Where we are in the surah

Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah has been sorting humanity into ranks. Ibn Kathir notes the movement simply: "After Allah mentioned the condition of those on the right hand, He then mentioned the condition of those on the left hand." So this passage is deliberately placed as a mirror to what came just before it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting on the two "large parties" of ayat 39–40, notes that the commentators differed over who "the earlier" and "the later" generations are. On one view, "the earlier" means the generations from Ādam (peace be upon him) up to the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and "the later" means the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ until the Day of Judgment. Read that way, Maʿārif says, it is a great honour for this ummah: despite the short period they lived in this world, they could be compared to all the previous communities before them, who were headed by hundreds of thousands of Prophets (peace be upon them). On the second view, both groups are from this ummah itself — and in that case, Maʿārif adds, though the Foremost grow fewer in the later generations, **the People of the Right will still be large in number in both the earlier and the later generations.** In support of this Maʿārif cites a hadith reported by **Bukhari and Muslim** from Sayyidnā Muʿāwiyah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A group of my Ummah will always remain on the truth and dominant, unharmed by those who fail to support them and those who defy them, until the Last Hour begins."

Hold that beside ayah 41 and the contrast is the whole point. Some are kept on the truth; others are about to be described.

## Ayah 41: a question that refuses to be answered plainly

**وَأَصْحَابُ الشِّمَالِ مَا أَصْحَابُ الشِّمَالِ** — "And the people of the left — how ˹miserable˺ will they be!"

The ayah names them, and then puts a question rather than a statement. Ibn Kathir renders it "And those on the left? How will be those on the left?" and explains that it means "What is the condition of those on the left" — after which, he says, Allah "explains His statement" in what follows.

So ayah 41 is not asking for information; it is stopping the listener. It is announced first and unpacked afterwards.

Notice, too, that the People of the Left are not introduced by their crimes. They are introduced by the side they stand on — Ibn Kathir's whole discussion runs on that contrast, "those on the right hand" and "those on the left hand." Their sins come only at the end of the passage, in ayat 45–46, once we already know what standing there costs.

## Ayat 42–44: three things that should have helped, and don't

Then the answer comes, and it comes as three descriptions in a row.

**فِي سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ — "in Samūm and Ḥamīm" (42).** Ibn Kathir glosses *samūm* as **"a fierce hot wind,"** and *ḥamīm* as **"boiling water."** Both are things that in ordinary life bring relief; here both have been turned into instruments. The wind scorches instead of cooling. The water boils instead of quenching.

**وَظِلٍّ مِّن يَحْمُومٍ — "and a shade of Yaḥmūm" (43).** This is the cruellest turn in the passage. They are given *shade* — and it is a shade "of *yaḥmūm*." Ibn Kathir reports that this means **the shadow of smoke** — this from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, As-Suddī "and others." He then states it directly: *yaḥmūm* means **black smoke**.

Ibn Kathir brings a passage from Sūrat al-Mursalāt to open this up further, calling it "a similar statement," where Allah says: "Depart you to that which you used to deny! Depart you to a shadow in three columns, neither shady nor of any use against the fierce flame of the Fire. Verily, it throws sparks like fortresses, as if they were yellow camels or bundles of ropes. Woe that Day to the deniers" (77:29–34). That is the point exactly — a shade that gives no shade. It has the shape of mercy and none of the substance.

**لَّا بَارِدٍ وَلَا كَرِيمٍ — "neither cool nor refreshing" (44).** Now the shade is defined by what it lacks. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that it **"neither brings soft, cool breeze nor appears clear."**

*Karīm* is the harder word, and the commentators handled it in slightly different ways, which is worth seeing rather than flattening:

- **Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah** said of *wa lā karīm*: **"Its sight is not pleasant."** That is, it is ugly to look at — nothing about it gives any comfort even to the eye.
- **Ad-Daḥḥāk** said: **"Every drink that is not fresh, is not *karīm* (pleasant),"** reading the word in terms of what is wholesome and good to receive.

Read together, the two comments touch on both the seeing and the receiving of a thing. So ayah 44 is saying: this shade has neither of the qualities shade exists for. Not cool. Not good. Just black smoke going by the name of shade.

There is a quiet lesson in that construction. In this world, the false often wears the shape of the true — comfort that is not comfort, safety that is not safety. On that Day the shape and the substance finally match.

## Ayat 45–46: why they are there

The passage does not leave the punishment hanging as raw terror. Ibn Kathir marks the transition himself: "Then, Allah the Exalted stated that they deserve this end." Two causes are named.

**إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا قَبْلَ ذَٰلِكَ مُتْرَفِينَ — "Indeed, before this ˹torment˺ they were spoiled by luxury" (45).** Ibn Kathir's gloss: **"in the life of the world, they were enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts, all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them."**

Read that carefully, because it is easy to misread the ayah as a condemnation of wealth as such. That is not what Ibn Kathir describes. His gloss has three parts, and the fatal one is the last: *all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them*. The enjoying and the satisfying are set against what was being ignored while they went on. Comfort became the whole horizon, and revelation was pushed aside. Note also the ayah's own phrase, **"before that"** — before the smoke, before the boiling water. Those pleasures are placed deliberately next to what came after them.

**وَكَانُوا يُصِرُّونَ عَلَى الْحِنثِ الْعَظِيمِ — "and persisted in the worst of sin" (46).** Two things are being said.

First, *yuṣirrūn* — persisting. Ibn Kathir: they **"persisted and did not intend to repent."** That is the sharpest word in the passage for a believer to sit with. What is named is not simply that they fell into sin, but that they stayed in it with no intention of turning back.

Second, *al-ḥinth al-ʿaẓīm* — "the great sin." Ibn Kathir specifies it: it is **"disbelief in Allah and claiming that the idols and rivals were gods besides Allah"** — that is, idolatry (*shirk*). He reports this as the meaning given by **Ibn ʿAbbās**, and adds that the same meaning is reported from **Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Qatādah, As-Suddī and others.**

## What follows, and what it tells us about these six ayat

The ayat immediately after complete the portrait, and Ibn Kathir treats the whole block as one. They used to say, "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we then indeed be resurrected? And also our forefathers?" (56:47–48) — saying it, Ibn Kathir notes, "while denying and rejecting the idea that resurrection will ever occur." The answer given is that the earlier and later generations of the Children of Ādam will all be gathered for the Day of Resurrection "and none of them will be left out," at "the appointed meeting of a known Day" — a time, Ibn Kathir says, that "is precisely designated and will not come late, early, nor increase or decrease."

Then comes the food and the drink: seized and made to eat from the tree of Zaqqūm until their stomachs are full, and boiling water drunk on top of it, drunk **"like al-hīm."** Ibn Kathir reports that *ḥamīm* is boiling water and *al-hīm* means **thirsty camels**, on the authority of **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and ʿIkrimah**. **As-Suddī** offered a different picture: *al-hīm*, he said, is "a disease that strikes camels, causing them to feel thirst, and they drink until they die" — and on that basis, Ibn Kathir reports, As-Suddī concluded that the people of Hell "will never quench their thirst from drinking Ḥamīm."

And the whole of it is then called **their *nuzul*** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "their entertainment on the Day of Recompense," which he paraphrases: "this, what We have described, is their entertainment with their Lord on the Day of their Reckoning." Ibn Kathir then points to the same word used of the believers — "those who believe and do righteous good deeds shall have the Gardens of Al-Firdaws for their *nuzul*" (18:107) — which he explains as **"hospitality and honor."** The word is the same for both, and the bitterness is in that symmetry: this smoke, this scalding, is what has been laid out to receive them.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of an intelligent, honest reader.

**Do not let comfort become the horizon.** Ayah 45, as Ibn Kathir explains it, describes people "enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts, all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them." The diagnostic question is not how comfortable your life is, but whether that comfort has quietly displaced revelation as the thing you organise your days around.

**Never let a sin become a settlement.** Ayah 46's word is *persisting* — "they persisted and did not intend to repent." Failing and returning is the human pattern; failing and intending never to return is what this ayah names.

**Test what you are sheltering under.** Ayat 43–44 give a shade that is neither cool nor good — comfort in name only. It is worth asking, calmly, of the things we take shelter in: is this shade, or is it smoke shaped like shade?

And ayah 41's question still stands over all of it. Allah does not first tell us what these people did; He tells us where they end up, and only then why. The order is a mercy — because we are still on the side of the passage where the *why* can be changed.

passages.title: The deniers mock resurrection and are answered
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat put a sneer on record and then answer it. In ayat 47–48 we hear the words of the people of the left hand — a mocking question about being raised after death — and in ayat 49–50 Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to reply: earlier and later generations alike will be gathered for the appointed meeting of a known Day. What binds the unit together is that pairing: the objection quoted, and the reply that answers it in full.

## The immediate lead-in

Ibn Kathir reads these ayat inside the surah's account of the people of the left hand. Just before the mockery is quoted, two things are said about them.

Ayah 45: "Verily, before that, they indulged in luxury" — Ibn Kathir explains that this means that in the life of the world "they were enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts, all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them."

Ayah 46: they "were persisting in great sin." Persisting, Ibn Kathir says, means "they persisted and did not intend to repent." The "great sin" is "disbelief in Allah and claiming that the idols and rivals were gods besides Allah." That it means idolatry is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and likewise from Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, As-Suddi and others.

That is the company the mockery of ayah 47 keeps in Ibn Kathir's reading: it is quoted as part of the description of these same people.

## What they used to say (ayat 47–48)

Their words are given in two stages.

**Ayah 47:** "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we then indeed be resurrected?"

**Ayah 48:** "And also our forefathers?"

Ibn Kathir's comment on the two ayat together is short and exact: "They said this while denying and rejecting the idea that resurrection will ever occur." So this was not an inquiry looking for an answer. It carried its own verdict inside it — a denial in the shape of a question.

## The answer: an instruction to announce (ayah 49)

The reply does not open with a proof. It opens with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: **"Say."**

Ibn Kathir gives the sense: "Say, O Muhammad, that the earlier and latter generations of the Children of Adam will be gathered for the Day of Resurrection and none of them will be left out."

Two things are worth noticing.

**First, the scope.** They had asked about themselves and then about their forefathers. The answer names "those of old, and those of later times" — the earlier and the latter generations of the children of Adam, with, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "none of them left out." Nothing in the objection is trimmed down to make the reply easier; the answer is given at full size.

**Second, the form.** The Prophet ﷺ is told to state it. This is a matter of what Allah has informed us will happen, and its certainty rests on the One informing.

## A gathering at a known time (ayah 50)

"All will surely be gathered together for appointed meeting of a known Day."

Ibn Kathir explains why the Day is described as *known*: "because that time is precisely designated and will not come late, early, nor increase or decrease."

Sit with that for a moment. Not vague, not approximate, not a maybe. A time so exactly fixed that it cannot slip forward or back, cannot stretch or shrink.

Ibn Kathir places a passage from Surah Hud alongside it: "That is a Day whereon mankind will be gathered together, and that is a Day when all will be present. And We delay it only for a term fixed. On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His leave. Some among them will be wretched and (others) blessed" (11:103–105). The same notes sound in both places: everyone gathered; the delay is a fixed term, not an oversight; and when the Day arrives, no one speaks except by His leave.

## "Earlier and later generations"

The pair *al-awwalun wa al-akhirun* — earlier and later — runs through this surah. Maʿarif ul Qurʼan, discussing the same two terms where they appear earlier in the surah (56:39–40, "many from the earlier generations, and many from the later ones"), records that the commentators held two views about who is meant.

On the **first view**, "the earlier" refers to the generations from Adam (peace be upon him) down to the period just before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, and "the later generations" refers to the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ until the Day of Judgment. Maʿarif notes what an honour this would be for this ummah: despite the short period it lived in this world, it could be compared to all the previous communities combined — communities headed, as Maʿarif puts it, by hundreds of thousands of Prophets (peace be upon them). Maʿarif adds that the wording "many from the later generations" even has the scope of being larger in number than "many from the earlier generations."

On the **second view**, both "earlier" and "later" refer to generations within the ummah of the Prophet ﷺ itself. On this reading, Maʿarif observes, even the later generations of this ummah will not be totally deprived of the Foremost, though their number will be less; and as for the People of the Right, their number will be large in both earlier and later generations. Maʿarif cites in support a hadith reported by Bukhari and Muslim from Sayyidna Muʿawiyah (may Allah be pleased with him), in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "A group of my ummah will always remain on the truth and dominant, unharmed by those who fail to support them and those who defy them, until the Last Hour begins."

In ayat 49–50 the same two words are used of the gathering itself: earlier and later, with none of them left out.

## Living it

**Ease can quietly crowd out revelation.** Ibn Kathir's phrase about the people described in ayah 45 is worth keeping: they were "enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts, all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them." Enjoyment is not the problem named there; the ignoring is.

**Persisting is what ayah 46 condemns, and Ibn Kathir defines it precisely:** "they persisted and did not intend to repent." The exit from that description is not a spotless record; it is the intention to turn back.

**Take the appointment seriously because it is an appointment.** Ayah 50 speaks of a gathering "for appointed meeting of a known Day" — a time, in Ibn Kathir's words, that "will not come late, early, nor increase or decrease."

**And do not measure Allah's power by what seems recoverable.** The objection in ayat 47–48 rested on dust and bones, and then on ancestors long gone. The answer concedes nothing to it: "those of old, and those of later times," none of them left out, at a known hour.

passages.title: Zaqqūm and boiling water for the deniers
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the final panel in the portrait of the People of the Left — one of the groups Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah sorts humanity into, alongside those on the right hand and the Foremost. Having described what the deniers will find waiting for them, Allah now turns and speaks to them directly, and lays out what they will eat, what they will drink, and then names the whole thing with a single word.

What holds ayat 51–56 together is that Ibn Kathir treats them as one continuous passage. Ayah 51 calls out those addressed; 52–53 give them their food; 54–55 their drink; and 56 names what has just been described — "this is their *nuzul*", rendered by Ibn Kathir as their "entertainment". Read as a unit, the passage is a single, terrible act of hospitality.

## The run-up: how the passage arrives here (ayat 41–50)

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. After Allah mentioned the condition of those on the right hand, He mentioned the condition of those on the left: "And those on the left — how will be those on the left?" — meaning, what is their condition? Then He explains it. They are in **Samūm**, which Ibn Kathir explains as a fierce hot wind; in **Ḥamīm**, boiling water; and under "a shadow from **Yaḥmūm**" — the shadow of smoke, black smoke, as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others.

That word "shadow" is where the cruelty of the image sits. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the parallel scene in Sūrah al-Mursalāt: "Depart you to that which you used to deny! Depart you to a shadow in three columns, neither shady nor of any use against the fierce flame of the Fire" (77:29–34). The verse itself makes the point: this is a shadow that gives no shade and shields from nothing. Allah adds here: "neither *bārid* nor *karīm*" — Ibn Kathir explains it neither brings a soft, cool breeze nor appears clear. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said of *karīm* here: "Its sight is not pleasant." Ad-Daḥḥāk said that every drink that is not fresh is not *karīm* — not pleasant.

Then Ibn Kathir notes that Allah states why they deserve this end, and it is worth pausing on, because ayat 51–56 are the sentence and ayat 45–46 are the verdict behind it:

- **"Verily, before that, they indulged in luxury"** — *mutrafīn*. Ibn Kathir: in the life of this world they were enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts, all the while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them. Note where the charge falls in his wording: enjoyment *with the Messengers' message ignored*.
- **"And were persisting"** — Ibn Kathir: they persisted and did not intend to repent. Not a slip, but a settled refusal to turn back.
- **"in *al-ḥinth al-ʿaẓīm*, the great sin"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as disbelief in Allah and claiming that idols and rivals were gods besides Him; it means idolatry (*shirk*), according to Ibn ʿAbbās, and this is also the meaning reported from Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ad-Daḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others.

And their signature argument, quoted in ayat 47–48: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we then indeed be resurrected? And also our forefathers?" They said this, Ibn Kathir notes, while denying and rejecting the idea that resurrection would ever occur. The answer comes in ayat 49–50: say, O Muhammad ﷺ, that the earlier and later generations of the Children of Ādam will be gathered for the Day of Resurrection, and none of them will be left out. Ibn Kathir draws out the phrase "an appointed meeting of a known Day": that time is precisely designated — it will not come late or early, nor increase or decrease. He brings the parallel from Sūrah Hūd: "That is a Day whereon mankind will be gathered together, and that is a Day when all will be present. And We delay it only for a term fixed. On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His leave. Some among them will be wretched and (others) blessed" (11:103–105).

So the argument is closed before ayah 51 begins. They said resurrection is impossible; Allah says it is scheduled, and scheduled exactly.

## Ayah 51: the address turns to face them

**"Then you, O misguided deniers…"**

Notice what happens to the speech itself. Through ayat 45–48 the deniers are being talked *about* — "they indulged", "they were persisting", "they used to say". Here they are addressed directly: **innakum**, "you". Ibn Kathir renders the address "you the erring-ones, the deniers."

Two names are placed on them:

- **aḍ-ḍāllūn**, rendered "the misguided" in the translation and "the erring-ones" by Ibn Kathir.
- **al-mukadhdhibūn**, the deniers — those who called the truth a lie. This is exactly the posture Ibn Kathir describes at ayat 47–48: they said what they said "while denying and rejecting the idea that resurrection will ever occur." It is also the word that closes the passage Ibn Kathir cites from Sūrah al-Mursalāt: "Woe that Day to the deniers" (77:29–34).

The ayah names them by both, and it names them at the moment the appointed meeting of ayah 50 has arrived.

## Ayat 52–53: the food

**"…will certainly eat from the trees of Zaqqūm, filling up your bellies with it."**

Ibn Kathir's comment on ayat 51–53 is short and heavy: this indicates that **they will be seized and made to eat** from the Zaqqūm tree until their stomachs become full. Two things stand out.

First, *seized and made to eat*. In the world they chose their meals; here, in Ibn Kathir's wording, the eating is not chosen at all. The *mutrafīn* of ayah 45 — the people who were enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their lusts — are now made to eat something else entirely.

Second, *until their stomachs become full*. Ayah 53 does not say they nibble at it. **fa-māliʾūna minhā al-buṭūn** — "filling up your bellies with it." Eating in the world stops when you are full; here the filling is the punishment itself.

## Ayat 54–55: the drink

**"Then on top of that you will drink boiling water — and you will drink it like thirsty camels do."**

*Ḥamīm*, Ibn Kathir states plainly, is boiling water. And ayah 54 says **ʿalayhi** — "on top of it", on top of the Zaqqūm already filling the belly. This is why the passage must be read as one unit: the drink is not a separate torment listed beside the food, it is poured onto it.

Then ayah 55 gives the image that fixes the whole scene: **shurb al-hīm**. Ibn Kathir reports the meaning of *al-hīm* from the early authorities:

- **Thirsty camels** — this is the meaning reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and ʿIkrimah.
- **A disease that strikes camels** — as-Suddī said: "Al-Hīm is a disease that strikes camels, causing them to feel thirst, and they drink until they die."

Ibn Kathir then draws the conclusion out of as-Suddī's reading: therefore, he said, the people of Hell will never quench their thirst from drinking the *ḥamīm*. That is where the simile lands. A normal drink ends thirst. This one is drunk in the manner of a creature whose thirst is not ended by drinking at all — the drinking never arrives at relief.

## Ayah 56: the word that reframes everything

**"This will be their accommodation on the Day of Judgment."**

The Arabic is **hādhā nuzuluhum** — and *nuzul* is the sting of the passage. Ibn Kathir renders it "entertainment": this, what We have described, is their entertainment with their Lord on the Day of their Reckoning.

He makes the point unmistakable by putting the believers' verse next to it: "Verily, those who believe and do righteous good deeds, shall have the Gardens of al-Firdaws (Paradise) for their entertainment" — *nuzulan* (18:107) — which he glosses as "hospitality and honor." So *nuzul* is the word for what is set out to receive someone. For one group, the Gardens of Firdaws are that reception. For the other, the reception is Zaqqūm and boiling water.

Ibn Kathir keeps the word in that plain sense — their entertainment **with their Lord** on the Day of their Reckoning — on the Day named here **yawm ad-dīn**, the Day of Recompense.

Notice too that ayah 56 leaves the direct address of ayat 51–55 behind: it does not say "your accommodation" but "**their** accommodation." The one hearing these words now is left looking at the scene rather than standing inside it.

## What this passage asks of us

The sources let us say three things concretely, and no more.

**Take the diagnosis of ayat 45–46 seriously.** Ibn Kathir does not say they were destroyed for having comfort; he says they were enjoying life's pleasures and satisfying their desires *while ignoring what the Messengers brought to them*. In his wording, the fatal element is the ignoring, not the enjoying.

**Break the persistence.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on "and were persisting" is that they persisted **and did not intend to repent**. The intention to turn back is the hinge. A sin with repentance still intended is a different thing from a sin one has decided never to leave. And since the appointed Day has not yet come, that hinge is still within reach.

**Let the certainty land.** Ibn Kathir stresses that the meeting-time of ayah 50 is precisely designated — it will not come late, early, nor increase or decrease. The people of this passage staked everything on the claim that dust and bones do not come back. In ayat 51–56 they are not met with a counter-argument; they are met with a meal.

And one last thing worth holding onto. The word *nuzul* in ayah 56 is the same word Allah uses in 18:107 for the Gardens of Firdaws, which Ibn Kathir explains as hospitality and honour. One word, two receptions. Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah leaves us with the question of which one is ours.

passages.title: Your own creation proves the resurrection
passages.tafsir:
Six ayat that answer a denial with a question. Earlier in the surah the deniers had said, *"When we die and become dust and bones, shall we then indeed be resurrected?"* (56:47) — said, as Ibn Kathir puts it, in denial and discounting Resurrection. Allah does not answer with a lecture on the Last Day. He points them back at their own bodies. What holds ayat 57–62 together is a single line of reasoning walked from end to end: you were nothing and then you were something; you had no hand in it; death is decreed over you and cannot be escaped; and the One who did all this the first time is not going to be frustrated the second time.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks ayah 57 as the beginning of a series of arguments in support of Allah's Oneness and His power to raise the dead. Up to this point the surah has been describing the three categories of people on the Plain of Hashr (the Plain of Gathering) and the reward and punishment of those three groups. From here the address turns to the sceptics and deniers themselves — those who completely deny the Day of Judgement and life after death, or who set up partners to Allah in His worship. And the argument does not stop at ayah 62; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that from ayah 63 onwards the surah gives a brief account of the three principal things upon which man's life in this world depends — food, water and fire, with food being the subject of ayah 63. Before those, the surah begins where it does because of what ayat 57–62 are about: the birth of man from a very insignificant beginning. The nearest sign is *you*.

## The veil over the obvious

Before going through the ayat, it is worth sitting with the diagnosis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers, because it explains why a proof this plain does not land. These ayat, it says, are meant to tear down the curtain of negligence and ignorance that has kept man in the dark.

Whatever exists, or is coming into existence now, or will come into existence later in this cosmic world, is the result of the creative power of Allah. He brings things into existence, He retains them in existence, and He makes them subservient to man. But the apparent causes of these events act as veils over Reality. Allah, with His encompassing power and consummate wisdom, has created a strong connection between causes and effects, so that wherever and whenever a secondary cause occurs, the effect necessarily follows. So the casual observer assigns every effect to a secondary or extrinsic cause, and strays into the philosophy of causes and effects — never realising that the whole system of cause and effect ends with Allah, the Cause of all causes (*musabbib al-asbāb*).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the logic: every cause that is not itself primary is traceable to some other cause, and that to another, and so on. But the series of cause and effect in our finite world cannot be indefinite; it must terminate at some point. The Final Cause is therefore the Author of the universe. And it is this Final Cause, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, towards which these ayat call our attention.

Why did Allah not simply remove the veils, so that a person could witness creation directly, without the mediation of apparent causes, and be forced to believe? Because, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers, Allah has made this world a venue of test. Therefore whatever comes into existence comes under the veils of causes. The Qur'an's work here is to lift the corner of one of them.

## Ayah 57 — "It is We Who created you"

**نَحۡنُ خَلَقۡنَٰكُمۡ فَلَوۡلَا تُصَدِّقُونَ**

*It is We Who created you. Will you not then believe ˹in resurrection˺?*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and total: *We have created you after you were nothing.* Hold that phrase — before Allah made you, there was no you at all. Then Ibn Kathir turns it into the question the whole passage is built on: **is not the One Who is able to start the creation more able to bring it back?**

On the closing words, the two commentaries give complementary renderings. Ibn Kathir renders them *"then why do you believe not?"* and supplies the object left unspoken: *why do you not then believe in Resurrection?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders them *"then why do you not appreciate it as true?"* — that is, to credit it as true, to stop calling it a lie. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah then goes on to bring forth evidence that Resurrection occurs. The evidence is being laid in front of them; what is asked of them is that they hold it true.

## Ayat 58–59 — the drop you had nothing to do with

**أَفَرَءَيۡتُم مَّا تُمۡنُونَ ۞ ءَأَنتُمۡ تَخۡلُقُونَهُۥٓ أَمۡ نَحۡنُ ٱلۡخَٰلِقُونَ**

Ibn Kathir renders it *"Do you not see the semen you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the opening as a direct summons: *"So, tell Me about the semen you drop [in the wombs]."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this the first argument in the series, and says it is taken from the very subtle and wonderful phenomenon of man's birth, starting with a drop of semen and developing into a full-fledged human being — the crown of all creation. The reason the Qur'an picks this particular sign is stated plainly: **humans stop at thinking that male–female cohabitation in the process of their creation is the ultimate or real cause.** That is the veil. So the Qur'an poses its question at exactly that point: is it *you* who create it, or are We the Creator?

Ibn Kathir unfolds what is being asked: *do you make the semen remain in the wombs and create life from it therein, stage after stage? Or is Allah the One Who does all this?*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then follows the process out, and the effect is deliberately humbling. The male plays a very insignificant biological role — he delivers a drop of microscopic semen into the womb of a female to combine with the microscopic ovum. Once this is done, it goes through several stages of growth and development without anyone besides Allah knowing what is happening. Eventually it forms into a foetus with a bone structure; the skeleton is then clothed with flesh and skin; the soul is infused into it. And the little universe — the microcosm — comes into being with its various systems: the nutritive and digestive system, the blood and circulatory system, the human senses of sight, touch, smell, hearing and taste, communication, and the ability to think and understand. Man thus becomes, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase, a moving factory — and **in none of these biological processes does he have any say.**

Then come the questions, meant to be felt rather than answered: who creates the child in the womb of the mother, creation after creation, within three darknesses — the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb and the darkness of the amniotic membrane? Who made it beautiful, and gave it the power of hearing and sight? Who bestowed on it the faculty of thinking and comprehension? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail anyone who has waited on a birth will recognise: neither of the parents — especially the mother, in whose womb all of this is taking place — knows whether the child is a boy or a girl until it is born. If the parents are that far outside the work, whose work is it? Only a mentally blind person, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, will fail to exclaim: *"Blessed is Allah, the Best of Creators!"*

The two ayat leave the denier nowhere to stand. He cannot claim he made himself. And if he did not make himself the first time, his confidence about what cannot happen a second time is not knowledge.

## Ayah 60 — death, decreed and undodgeable

**نَحۡنُ قَدَّرۡنَا بَيۡنَكُمُ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ وَمَا نَحۡنُ بِمَسۡبُوقِينَ**

Having shown that the beginning of life is not ours, the passage turns to its end — which is not ours either. Ibn Kathir: *We made death exist between you.* Ad-Dahhak commented: **"Allah made the residents of the heavens and earth equal with regards to death."** Death is not a peculiarly human misfortune; the decree runs across the creation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this does to a person's sense of his own security. Death is the end of all physical life — the eternal law of Allah from which there is no escape. Allah pre-determines the time of human death; man has no choice in the matter, and Allah has pre-designated a particular point in time up to which he could live, at which the soul is freed from the fetters and shackles of its physical habitat. So one should not remain lulled into a fancy that he will continue to enjoy his power and his free will. Allah has the power to eliminate him at any time, and to create another people in his place.

**Wa mā naḥnu bi-masbūqīn** — rendered by Ibn Kathir *"and We are not outstripped,"* meaning, in his gloss, *'We are never unable.'* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words *"and We cannot be frustrated."*

## Ayah 61 — replaced, transfigured, remade

**عَلَىٰٓ أَن نُّبَدِّلَ أَمۡثَٰلَكُمۡ وَنُنشِئَكُمۡ فِي مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ**

This ayah completes the sentence begun in ayah 60: We are not outstripped *as regards doing this*. The two commentaries read "this" in complementary ways, and it is worth keeping both.

**Ibn Kathir** reads it of the Hereafter: "to transfigure you" means *to change your current shapes, on the Day of Resurrection*, and "and create you in that you know not" he glosses as *out of shapes and forms*. On this reading the ayah is a direct statement about the Resurrection itself — the same person, raised, but not in a mould you can picture from where you now stand.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads the first half in continuity with ayah 60: *"We cannot be frustrated from replacing you with others like you"* — a generation removed and successors raised in its place. On the closing words it says the implication is that Allah has the power to reshape you in a form unknown to you at the moment. It offers more than one way this may happen: either by one's turning into dust after death, or by being metamorphosed into an animal shape as happened in past nations, some turned into monkeys and others into swine by way of punishment; and it adds that it is also possible that they might be transformed into stones or minerals.

Both readings touch the same nerve. Your present form is not a fixture. The One who assigned it can assign another — in this world by replacing you with others like you, and on that Day by raising you in a form you do not know.

## Ayah 62 — you have already seen this done once

**وَلَقَدۡ عَلِمۡتُمُ ٱلنَّشۡأَةَ ٱلۡأُولَىٰ فَلَوۡلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ**

*You already know how you were first created. Will you not then remember?*

Here the argument closes, and it closes not by demanding a new belief but by asking for a memory. Ibn Kathir: *you know that Allah has created you after you were nothing. He created you and gave you hearing, sight and hearts. Will you not then remember and take heed that He Who is able to create you in the beginning is more able to bring you back and resurrect you to life anew?*

The first creation is not a doctrine anyone has to be argued into; the ayah addresses it as something the listener already knows. The Resurrection is not asking you to believe in something unprecedented. It is asking you to take heed of a precedent you are living inside.

Ibn Kathir gathers other ayat where the Qur'an makes this same move, and reading them together is the fastest way to feel how central it is:

- *"And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him."* (30:27)
- *"Does not man remember that We created him before, while he was nothing?"* (19:67)
- *"Does not man see that We have created him from a nuṭfah [a drop]? Yet behold, he stands forth as an open opponent. And he puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation.'"* (36:77–79)
- *"Does man think that he will be left neglected? Was he not a nuṭfah of semen emitted? Then he became an ʿalaqah [a clot]; then shaped and fashioned in due proportion… Is not He able to give life to the dead?"* (75:36–40)

That last one adds the thought the surah has been circling. The alternative to resurrection is not peace; it is being left neglected — made for nothing.

## Living it

**Stop the chain of causes at the right place.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about veils is not abstract. When we explain a birth, a recovery, a salary, a rescue, we name the nearest cause and fall silent — and that silence is where tawḥīd (holding Allah to be One, with no partner in His lordship or worship) quietly leaks away. The correction is not to deny causes, which Allah Himself bound so firmly to their effects, but to keep following them home to the Cause of all causes.

**Let your own body be the evidence.** These ayat put the proof of the Resurrection inside the person being addressed. Whoever wants certainty about it is told to think about a drop, a womb, three darknesses, and a hearing, seeing, thinking creature that came out of it — none of which he arranged.

**Take the decree of death seriously while you can still act on it.** Ayah 60 says the time is pre-determined and there is no escape from it, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns explicitly against the fancy that our present power and free will will simply keep running.

**Treat forgetfulness as the real problem.** Ayah 62 does not tell the deniers something new. It asks them to remember and take heed of what they already know. That is what makes this passage recitable rather than merely arguable: every time you read it, it hands you back your own beginning as evidence of your own return.

passages.title: The sign of the crop you sow
passages.tafsir:
These ayat take the most ordinary thing in an agricultural society — a field of grain — and turn it into an argument for the Oneness of Allah. Ibn Kathir titles this whole section "Allah's Oneness demonstrated by causing the Plants to grow, sending down the Rain and creating the Fire that Mankind needs." Ayat 63–67 are the first of those three proofs. They hold together as a single movement: a question about who really grows your food (63–64), a reminder of how easily it could be taken away (65), and then the words that would fall out of your own mouth if it were (66–67).

## The question that reopens a closed case

Ayah 63 begins with *a-fa-ra'aytum* — "Have you considered…", "Do you not see…". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is the Qur'an's characteristic method here: it poses a question to man, and the question is built so that the answer, once you actually think it through, is obvious.

Ibn Kathir explains *mā taḥruthūn* — "what you sow" — as "tilling the earth and planting seeds inside it." That is the whole of what the verb names: breaking the soil, putting the seed in. Then ayah 64 asks the decisive question: *a-antum tazraʿūnahu am naḥnu z-zāriʿūn* — "Is it you who cause it to grow, or is it We Who do so?" Ibn Kathir paraphrases the first half as "do you cause these seeds to grow inside the earth?" and gives Allah's own answer to the second: "rather it is We Who cause the seeds to remain firmly and grow inside the earth."

Notice what has happened between the two ayat. The Qur'an has separated one process into two verbs and handed them to two different agents. *Ḥarth* — tilling and sowing — is yours; the ayah says so plainly, *mā taḥruthūn*, "what **you** sow." *Zarʿ* — causing to grow — is not yours, and ayah 64 asks the question in a way that leaves only one honest answer.

## "Do not say: I made it grow"

The Prophet ﷺ made this distinction a rule of speech. Ibn Jarir recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Do not say, *Zaraʿtu* (I made it grow), but say, *Ḥarathtu* (I sowed, I tilled)."

And Abu Hurayrah then added: "Have you not heard Allah's statement, *Do you not see what you sow. Is it you that make it grow, or are We the Grower?*"

This is worth pausing over. A farmer saying "I grew this wheat" is not, on the face of it, an obvious offence — it is simply how people talk. Yet the Prophet ﷺ asked that even this be corrected, and Abu Hurayrah understood immediately that the instruction came straight out of this ayah. The correction is small and constant, and it draws the same line the two ayat draw: *I sowed. He grew it.*

## The farmer's actual job description

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out with real care exactly how much of the harvest is the farmer's doing. He ploughs the land. He fertilizes the soil with manure. He softens the earth so that if the seed germinates, the shoot will not be hampered by hard ground. Once the plant sprouts, he takes care of it in that direction. And that is it — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, all of man's efforts move around this one point.

What man cannot claim is the germination itself: "man is not the primary cause of the shoots pushing forth from the seed nor can he claim that he made the plant or tree." So the question returns in its sharpest form — who caused a seed lying under heaps and heaps of sand to germinate and come out to the surface of the earth so beautifully, comprising untold benefits? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that there can be only one answer: the All-Encompassing Power and the Most Wonderful creation of the Master Creator of the universe.

And this is the diagnosis Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers for the human condition here — that man "was lost in the secondary or extrinsic causes and lost sight of his Real Creator and Master, the Primary or Intrinsic Cause of his creation." The ayah does not deny the secondary causes — the ploughing, the manure, the softened ground are all named and all real. It asks who stands behind them.

## "If We willed…" — ayah 65

*Law nashā'u la-jaʿalnāhu ḥuṭāman* — "If We willed, We could simply reduce this harvest to chaff." *Ḥuṭām* is what Ibn Kathir renders as crumbled dry pieces: the crop turned brittle and worthless.

Ibn Kathir's comment on this ayah is unexpectedly tender. The standing crop, he says, is there because "We caused the seeds to grow with Our compassion and mercy and left them intact inside the earth as mercy for you. If We will, We would turn them dry before they ripen and get ready to be harvested."

Two things follow. First, the harvest you are about to reap is not a neutral outcome of competent farming; Ibn Kathir calls it compassion and mercy, and mercy that is sustained — the crop was *left intact* for you. Second, the timing named here is severe by design: *before they ripen and get ready to be harvested*. Not a seed that never sprouted, but a field nearly ready, lost at the last moment. Everything spent, nothing returned. That is the scenario the ayah puts in front of you.

## *Tafakkahūn*: the word that means two opposite things

*Fa-ẓaltum tafakkahūn* — "and you would spend the day *tafakkahūn*." The early authorities read this word in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir preserves the range rather than flattening it:

- **ʿIkrimah**: it means "you will blame each other (and yourselves)."
- **Al-Hasan, Qatadah and As-Suddi**: it means you would feel sorrow. Ibn Kathir adds what the grief would be over: what they had spent, or the sins they had committed in the past, which cost them the destruction of their plants.
- **Al-Kisā'i** made a linguistic observation: *tafakkaha* is "both the synonym and the antonym." The Arabs say *tafakkahtu*, he notes, to mean they have enjoyed something — and also to mean they have felt grief.

That last note is the key to the picture. The verb can carry the sense of relishing something, and here it is used of people standing before a ruined field. The word that could describe you savouring the fruit is turned to describe what you do with the loss instead.

And ʿIkrimah's reading sits alongside the others as its own distinct possibility: what fills the day after the crop fails may not be grief at all, but blame — of one another, and of yourselves.

## What you would actually say — ayat 66 and 67

Ibn Kathir explains that if Allah crumbled the plants into dry pieces, "you would be wondering regarding what happened," saying sometimes one thing and sometimes another. The Qur'an quotes both.

**Ayah 66: *innā la-mughramūn*.** Ibn Kathir glosses *mughramūn* as ruined. **Mujahid and ʿIkrimah** said it means "being the subject of revenge" — that something has been exacted from you. **Qatadah** captured the alternation between the two ayat exactly: "You would say, 'We were punished,' sometimes, and, 'We were deprived,' some other times."

**Ayah 67: *bal naḥnu maḥrūmūn*** — "Nay, but we are deprived," or as the translation renders it, "In fact, we have been deprived of our livelihood." Ibn Kathir's word for the state behind both sentences is *wondering* — people turning over what has happened and not settling on an account of it. First it is a penalty, something exacted; then, no — it is simply that we have been cut off.

This is the quiet brilliance of the passage. Allah does not need to describe the ruined field at all. He describes only what would come out of the mouths of the people standing in it — and in that unsettled, self-revising speech, the claim of ayah 64 is proved out of their own words. The moment the crop fails, nobody says "I failed to grow it." Both sentences are things done *to* them: *we were punished, we were deprived*. What good times let a person conceal, loss makes him say out loud — that he was never the one growing it.

## Living it

**Correct the sentence.** The Prophet ﷺ gave a concrete, repeatable practice: say "I sowed," not "I grew it." The modern equivalents are easy to find — *I built this, I earned this, I made this happen*. The instruction is not to deny your effort; tilling is real work, and the ayah credits it to you by name. It is to stop your tongue at the boundary of what you actually did.

**Read a full plate as mercy, not as arithmetic.** If the standing crop is compassion and mercy sustained (Ibn Kathir), then food on the table is not merely the output of wages and shopping. Ayah 65 exists so that you can see the harvest you did get against the background of the harvest that could have been chaff.

**Watch where you go when it fails.** Ayat 66–67 are a mirror held up to loss. Blaming one another and yourselves (ʿIkrimah), grieving what you spent, grieving past sins (Al-Hasan, Qatadah, As-Suddi) — the passage records all of it without contempt; the grief is real. But it lets you hear that even your complaint is an admission. *We were deprived* concedes a Giver.

## Where the passage is heading

Ayat 63–67 are the first of the three signs named in Ibn Kathir's heading for this section: the plants that grow, the rain that is sent down, and the fire that mankind needs. The water you drink (68–70) and the fire you kindle (71–73) follow, each posed in the same form — *have you considered…? did you do this, or did We?* — and each, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, with an obvious answer. The sequence ends where it was always going, with the command of ayah 74: *Then glorify with praises the Name of your Lord, the Most Great.* Which means the harvest of ayah 63 is not simply a lesson in humility. It is a summons. Look at the field, follow the question honestly, and the last word is not argument but praise.

passages.title: Water and fire as signs, then glorify
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are the closing movement of a series of questions Allah puts to the human being about the most ordinary things in his life. Having already asked about the seed he sows (ayat 63–67), Allah now asks about the water he drinks (68–70) and the fire he lights (71–73) — and then, in ayah 74, tells him what the only honest response to those questions is: *So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest.* What holds the passage together is a single argument, made in two movements and sealed with a command.

## The argument the questions are making

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole sequence around one human failing: man "was lost in the secondary or extrinsic causes and lost sight of his Real Creator and Master, the Primary or Intrinsic Cause of his creation." We live among the immediate causes — the plough, the well, the match — and mistake them for the source. The Qur'an's method here is not to argue us out of that; it is to take the very thing our hands are busy with and ask who is actually doing the work.

Take the farmer, the case just before our passage. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out how little of the process is really his: he ploughs the land, fertilises the soil with manure, and softens it "so that if the seed germinates, it will not be hampered by the hard ground." All of man's efforts, it says, move around this point. But he is not the primary cause of the shoots pushing forth from the seed, nor can he claim that he made the plant or the tree. So the question stands: who caused the seed lying under "heaps and heaps of sand" to germinate and come out to the surface of the earth "so beautifully, comprising untold benefits"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that there can be only one answer — the All-Encompassing Power of the Master Creator of the universe.

Ibn Kathir preserves how sharply the Prophet ﷺ wanted this felt in the way we speak. Ibn Jarir recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Do not say, 'Zaraʿtu' (I made it grow), but say, 'Harathtu' (I sowed, I tilled)."** Abu Hurayrah then asked, "Have you not heard Allah's statement," and quoted these very ayat as his proof. Sow, yes — that is your verb. *Grow* is not your verb. Ayat 68–73 simply extend that correction from the field to the water jug and the hearth.

## Water: ayat 68–70

**"Have you considered the water you drink?" (68)** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes why water comes at this point in the sequence: "Next to food, water is the most important thing upon which human life depends for its sustenance." Nothing is more taken for granted, and nothing is closer to death when it is withheld.

**"Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so?" (69)** The word rendered "the clouds" here is *al-Muzn*. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others explained it as meaning clouds. And note where the question places the human being: not at the reservoir or the irrigation channel, where he does have a role, but at the point where water comes down from the sky. Every system we build for water begins downstream of an act that is entirely Allah's. Ibn Kathir's comment is flat and final: Allah "is stating that indeed He is the One Who causes the rain to fall."

**"If We willed, We could make it salty. Will you not then give thanks?" (70)** The word is *ujāj*. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "salty, sour, undrinkable and unfit for growing plants" — not merely unpleasant but useless twice over, for the throat and for the field. This is the hinge of the whole water passage. The rain does not merely fall; it falls sweet. Sweetness is not a property water owes us. The same clouds could have delivered brine, and nothing in Allah's power would have been strained by it.

That is why the ayah ends not with an argument but with a rebuke shaped as a question: *falawlā tashkurūn* — why then do you not give thanks? Ibn Kathir paraphrases: "why do you not appreciate the favor Allah does for you by sending down the rain fresh, ready to consume." He then places alongside it Allah's words in Surah an-Nahl: *"From it you drink and from it (grows) the vegetation on which you send your cattle to pasture. With it He causes to grow for you the crops, the olives, the date palms, the grapes, and every kind of fruit. Verily, in this is indeed an evident proof and a manifest sign for people who give thought."* (16:10–11) One rainfall; a whole economy of mercies hanging off it.

## Fire: ayat 71–73

**"Have you considered the fire you kindle?" (71)** Notice what the ayah credits to you and what it does not. It speaks of the fire *you kindle* — Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as "the fire you start with the use of trees." The kindling is granted to be yours. The next ayah asks about everything that makes the kindling possible.

**"Is it you who produce its trees, or is it We Who do so?" (72)** Ibn Kathir gives the answer on Allah's behalf: "rather We have made kindling fire possible." He then supplies the concrete image the first listeners would have had in mind. The Arabs had two kinds of trees called *Al-Markh* and *Al-ʿAfar* that they used to ignite a fire: when they would rub a green branch from each of these two trees against the other, sparks of fire would come out of them. Consider what that means. A *green*, sap-filled branch — the least combustible thing imaginable — carries fire hidden inside it, placed there by Allah, waiting for a human hand to release it. The man rubbing the sticks feels like the maker of the flame. He is only the one who found it where Allah had already put it.

Ibn Kathir extends the same observation to stone: it is "out of Allah's kindness that He has made the quality of kindling fire in some elements, such as stones," light enough that people can carry them in their baggage on a journey and strike a flame at the campsite.

**"We have made it a reminder and a provision." (73)** Two purposes — one for the soul, one for the body.

*A reminder* — *tadhkirah*. Ibn Kathir reports that Mujahid and Qatadah said this means a reminder of the Hellfire; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses it as a reminder both of Allah's infinite power and of the fire of Hell. Every fire you light is a small, survivable sample of something you must not end up in. The cooking flame is not only useful; it is a message.

## From the Sunnah on that reminder

Qatadah said, "We were told that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **'O people, this fire of yours that you kindle, is but one part out of seventy parts of the fire of Hell.'** They said, 'O Allah's Messenger! This fire alone is sufficiently hot.' The Messenger ﷺ said: 'It was submerged in the water twice so that the Children of Adam would be able to benefit from it and draw closer to it.'" Ibn Kathir classes this narration from Qatadah as *Mursal* — a technical grading of hadith scholars that he does not unpack here — and immediately shows that the same teaching is preserved through named collections.

**Imam Ahmad recorded it in his Musnad** from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Verily, this fire of yours is one part out of seventy parts of the fire of Hell. It was struck twice against the sea, otherwise, Allah would not have made benefit in it for anyone." **Imam Malik also recorded** that Abu Hurayrah said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "The fire that the Children of Adam kindle is one part out of seventy parts of the fire of Hell." When they said, "O Allah's Messenger! This fire alone is sufficiently hot," he ﷺ replied: "(The fire of Hell) was made sixty-nine times hotter." Ibn Kathir adds that **al-Bukhari** collected this hadith from Malik, and **Muslim** from Abu az-Zinad.

Sit with the detail that our fire had to be tempered before we could live beside it. The heat you back away from is the cooled version. That is what ayah 73 means by calling it a reminder — the warning is not delivered in a sermon, it is built into the hearth.

## Who are the *muqwīn*?

The second half of ayah 73 calls fire *matāʿan lil-muqwīn*, an article of use or provision for the *muqwīn*. The early scholars read this word in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than flattening it.

**Travellers.** Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak and an-Nadr bin ʿArabi all said the meaning of *al-muqwīn* is travellers. Ibn Jarir chose this view too, noting the Arabic saying *Aqwat ad-Dār* — "the house has become empty" — said when its people have travelled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the root: *muqwīn* is derived from the infinitive *iqwāʼ*, from the root-word *qiwāʼ*, which means "waste, barren land, ruin or desert." Thus a *muqwī* is "a traveller or a wayfarer of a desert who alights to prepare his meals" — the man stopping in empty country with nothing around him but what he carried and what he can strike into flame.

**The hungry.** ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said that here *al-muqwī* means the hungry.

**Everyone.** Layth bin Abi Sulaym reported that Mujahid said it means "those who are present at their homes and travelers, for every kind of food that requires cooking by fire," and Ibn Abi Najih reported that Mujahid said it means all people who enjoy eating food cooked by fire — and something similar was mentioned from ʿIkrimah. Ibn Kathir judges this last explanation "more general than the previous," since those in their own locale and those travelling, whether rich or poor, all need fire "for cooking, heating and lighting purposes."

Why then does the ayah name the one stranded in open country, when everyone benefits? Ibn Kathir observes exactly this: Allah mentions this favour specifically in the case of travellers, even though everyone benefits from the fire. And he shows why it lands there — when a traveller needs fire at his campsite for cooking and heating, he takes out these substances and kindles it, and "he feels comfort next to the fire." At home the fire is furniture. In the desert, a man knows exactly what he has been given. Allah names the blessing where it is most keenly recognised.

## Ayah 74: the only fitting response

**"So glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest."** Everything in the passage runs to this.

Ibn Kathir explains why this ending fits these particular signs: glorify "the One by Whose ability these things opposites were created." He created the fresh, tasty water, "and had He willed, He would have created it salty like seawater." He also created the fire that burns, and made a benefit in it for His servants — "suitable for their livelihood in this life and as a warning and a punishment for them in the Hereafter." Water that could have been undrinkable but soothes; fire that destroys but serves. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole passage in the same spirit: all these creations are the result of Allah's power and wisdom.

The command itself is *sabbih*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "proclaim the purity of the name of your Lord, the Magnificent." It draws the conclusion plainly: the logical and rational conclusion of everything just considered should be for man to believe in the All-Encompassing Divine Power and in Allah's Oneness, and to declare the Purity of the Great Lord — "for that is the way to express His gratitude."

Notice how that answers ayah 70. There Allah asked, *will you not then give thanks?* Here, at the close, He tells us what thanks actually looks like. Gratitude is not a warm feeling about rain. It is proclaiming the purity of the Great Lord — the tongue and the heart returning the credit to its Owner.

## Living it

This passage is unusually practical, because its subject matter passes through your hands several times a day.

**Watch your verbs.** The correction the Prophet ﷺ gave about *zaraʿtu* and *harathtu* is a discipline of speech that reshapes the heart. Say what you actually did — I sowed, I struck, I turned it on — and leave the growing, the raining and the burning to the One who does them.

**Let the ordinary interrupt you.** Ayat 68 and 71 both open by asking you to *consider* — to look again at something you habitually look past. A glass of water is a question with only one answer. So is a flame.

**Taste the sweetness deliberately.** Ayah 70 puts the alternative in front of you: it could have been *ujāj*, salty and undrinkable. Every drinkable mouthful is a gift that did not have to be given in that form.

**Let fire remind you.** Mujahid and Qatadah read ayah 73 as pointing to the Hellfire, and the reports above tell us that even the heat we flinch from is the tempered fraction of it. Let that become fear that moves you, and gratitude that Allah has placed you, for now, beside the fire that cooks your food rather than the fire that punishes.

**Then say it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls ayah 74 the logical and rational conclusion of everything before it — not a thought to file away, but a command to obey. Having seen the water and the fire, glorify the Name of your Lord, the Greatest.

passages.title: Oath by the stars: this noble Qur'an
passages.tafsir:
Allah swears a mighty oath by the setting-places of the stars — and what He swears to is the Qur'an itself: that it is noble, that it is kept in a protected Book, that only the purified touch it, and that it descends from the Lord of all the worlds. The passage then turns on the audience (ayat 81–82): is *this* the discourse you take lightly — and is denial what you make of what you are given?

What holds the eight ayat together is a single sentence-shape: an oath, the thing sworn to, and the rebuke that follows from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out where this sits in the sūrah's argument. The verses before it put forward rational arguments for life after death by inviting attention to Allah's infinite power. The current verses prove the same fact a different way — by giving an authoritative reference: the Qur'an.

## "Fa-lā uqsimu" — the "No!" before the oath

The passage opens with a word that puzzles readers: *fa-lā uqsimu*, literally "so, no — I swear." Why a negation at the head of an oath?

Ibn Kathir is firm that the *lā* is not an extra character without meaning, "as some of the scholars of Tafsir say." Rather it is used at the beginning of an oath when the oath is a negation. He gives a living example: ʿĀʼishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said, "*Lā*, by Allah! Allah's Messenger ﷺ did not touch any woman's hand at all." The "No!" is not part of the swearing — it is the rejection of a claim, and then the oath comes to overturn it.

So the meaning, Ibn Kathir says, is: "No! I swear by the *mawāqiʿ* of the stars. The matter is not as you people claim — about the Qur'an — that it is a result of magic or sorcery; rather it is an Honorable Qur'an." Ibn Jarir reports the same from some of the scholars of the Arabic language: *fa-lā uqsimu* means "the matter is not as you people have claimed," and then Allah renews the oath again by saying, "I swear."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that scholars genuinely differed here. Some lexicologists say the *lā* is added only as an idiomatic expression carrying no sense of its own — Arabic said *lā wallāh* ("No, by Allah"), and pre-Islamic Arabic had *lā wa-abīk* ("No, by your father"). Others say that when the refutation of an addressee's hypothesis is intended, the *lā* is there to signify that the addressee's assumption is not correct, and the right thing is what follows. Either way, before Allah says a word about the Qur'an, He has already swept the accusation off the table.

## Swearing by where the stars go down

*Mawāqiʿ* (ayah 75) is the plural of *mawqiʿ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it refers to the points where, or the times when, the stars set. Mujahid said it means "the setting positions of the stars in the sky," and also said it refers to their rising and setting positions. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said the same, and Ibn Jarir preferred this; Qatadah also gave the simpler sense, "their positions."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the oath is tied to their *setting* rather than their shining. It notes the parallel in Sūrat an-Najm — "By the star when it goes down to set" — where the oath by the stars is likewise qualified by their setting-time. The wisdom underlying this, Maʿārif explains, is that when the stars set, their function seems to have been cut off from the horizon, and we witness the effects of their vanishing. That is the proof of their perishability and of their dependence on Divine power.

Then ayah 76: **"and this, if only you knew, is indeed a great oath."** Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic — this is a great vow that Allah is making; *if you knew the greatness of this vow, you would know the greatness of the subject of the vow*. The size of the oath is a measure of the worth of the Qur'an.

## What the oath is for (ayat 77–80)

Commenting on ayat 77–79, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān labels the structure plainly: verses 75–76 constituted the oath, and this set of verses is the *jawāb al-qasam* — the subject of the oath. The oath exists to carry these statements about the Qur'an; ayah 80 continues the same description.

**"Truly a noble Qur'an" (77).** Ibn Kathir: verily, this Qur'an that was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ is a Glorious Book. Maʿārif adds what the words are aimed at — the verse refutes the assumption of the pagans that this Book has been forged by a human being, or that it is speech inspired by the devil.

**"In a well-preserved Record" (78).** Ibn Kathir glosses *Maknūn* as "glorious; in a glorious, well-guarded, revered Book." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the "protected book" as *lawḥ maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet. What they were hearing recited was not improvised — it had an origin above this world, guarded before it ever reached human ears.

**"A revelation from the Lord of all worlds" (80).** Ibn Kathir: this Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of all that exists — "not as they say that it is magic, sorcery or poetry. Rather it is the truth, no doubt about it; there is none beyond it of useful truth."

## "Touched by none except the purified" (79)

This is the ayah the scholars worked hardest on, and the differences here are real ones, which the sources name.

**First: what does "it" refer to?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, lays out two grammatical possibilities.

- The phrase may qualify **the Preserved Tablet** of ayah 78. In that case "the purified ones" can refer only to the angels, and "not touched" cannot be taken in its literal sense of physical touch — it would rather mean *being aware of*: no one is aware of the Preserved Tablet and its contents except the purified angels. This interpretation is adopted in Bayān ul-Qurʼān as well.
- Or it may qualify **the Qur'an** — in which case the word "Qur'an" refers to the scrolls or scripts in which it is written, and "not touched" keeps its literal sense of physical touch by hand. The sense would be that the Script of the Qur'an is not touched by anyone except the purified angels who bring revelation to the Prophet ﷺ. Since this interpretation does not need to take "touch" in a figurative sense, Qurtubi and some other commentators have preferred it.

Ibn Jarir also narrated, by a chain reaching Ibn 'Abbas, that about "none touches it but the pure ones" he said: "The Book that is in heaven."

Imam Malik said that the best interpretation of ayat 77–78 he ever heard is what is mentioned in Sūrah ʿAbasa (80:13–16): it is recorded in scripts that are honoured, exalted and purified, in the hands of scribes who are honourable and righteous.

**Second: who are the *muṭahharūn*?** A large group of the Companions, their followers, and leading authorities on Qur'anic commentary said: **the angels** — purified of the dross and adulteration of sins. Al-ʿAwfi reported this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Kathir lists as saying the like Anas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, ad-Dahhak, Abu ash-Shaʿtha' Jabir bin Zayd, Abu Nahik, as-Suddi, ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam "and others." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names Anas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn 'Abbas for this view, and adds that Imam Malik adopted it too.

Ibn Zayd read the ayah as an answer to a specific slander: the Quraysh disbelievers claimed that the devils brought the Qur'an down, so Allah stated that only the pure ones touch it — as He said elsewhere, "And it is not the Shayāṭīn who have brought it down… Verily, they have been removed far from hearing it" (26:210–212). Ibn Kathir calls this "a good saying," and — importantly — says it does not contradict those before it.

Some commentators, by contrast, held that "the Qur'an" here refers to the copy of the Book that is in our hands, and that the *muṭahharūn* are people free from impurity: minor impurity (being without wudūʼ, cleansed by wudūʼ or tayammum) and major impurity (the state requiring ghusl). On this reading, although the ayah is a declarative sentence, it is in fact used in the sense of prohibiting people from touching the Qur'an while impure. This interpretation is placed on the text by ʿAṭāʼ, Ṭāwus, Sālim and Muhammad Bāqir; Qurtubi and Mazhari prefer it.

Qatadah held both horizons together: "None can touch it, with Allah, except the pure ones. However, in this life, the impure Zoroastrian and the filthy hypocrite touch it." He noted that in the recitation of Ibn Masʿud the wording is *mā yamassuhu illā al-muṭahharūn* — "it is not touched, except by the pure ones." And Abu al-ʿĀliyah turned the ayah back on the deniers: "It does not refer to you, because you are sinners!"

**The story of ʿUmar.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls it here: in the account of ʿUmar's (may Allah be pleased with him) embracing Islam, he asked his sister for the pages of the Qur'an; she recited this very ayah, refused to give him the pages, and said that only the pure ones can touch it. As a result he was forced to bathe, and then recited what was on them. Maʿārif notes that this incident lends support to the last interpretation.

## What this means in practice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carefully separates the ruling from the evidence for it. Because Ibn 'Abbas and others held a different view of the ayah, many scholars did not base the prohibition of touching the Qur'an without ablution on ayah 79 at all. They based it on the Traditions:

- Imam Malik cites as evidence, in his Muwaṭṭaʼ, the Prophet's ﷺ letter to ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, which contains: *lā yamass al-Qurʼāna illā ṭāhir* — "Only a clean one may touch the Qur'an."
- Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī gives further references — the Musnad of ʿAbdurrazzāq, Ibn Abī Dāwud and Ibn ul-Mundhir, Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardūyah — recording a Tradition on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) with the same wording.

On that basis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports:

1. The overwhelming majority of the Ummah and the four major schools concur that purity is a condition for touching the Qur'an: no *najāsah* (what the Sharīʿah declares filth) attached to the hand, and the person in the state of wudūʼ and not in *janābah*. Some jurists take the ayah and the Traditions to bear the same sense and use them as mutually supporting; others, on account of the divergence of interpretation among the Companions, exercised precaution over using the Qur'anic text as evidence and ruled on the strength of the Traditions alone. **The rulings do not differ — only the supporting evidence cited for them.**
2. If the Qur'an is in a cover sewn or permanently attached to it, an unclean person may not touch it without ablutions, according to all four major schools. If the covering is not permanently attached, Imam Abu Hanifah permits touching it without ablutions; Imams Malik and Shafiʿi do not.
3. A person who is unclean may not touch it with the sleeve or skirt of a garment he is wearing — but he may with a handkerchief or a sheet.
4. Scholars ruled that a person in *janābah*, and a woman in menstruation or postpartum bleeding, may not recite the Qur'an even from memory until ghusl has been taken: if it is obligatory to honour the written letters by touching them only in purity, the spoken words deserve that honour with greater importance still. Minor impurity is different — Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them) report that the Prophet ﷺ recited the Qur'an without wudūʼ, so the jurists ruled recitation without wudūʼ permissible, while the rule for major impurity remains intact.

## "Is it this discourse you take lightly?" (81)

Now the rebuke. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: "Is it this discourse that you take lightly?" Ibn Kathir renders it: "Is it such a talk that you are Mudhinun?"

The word *mudhinūn* is worth feeling. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it to *idhān*, which literally means to apply or rub oil on the body. When oil is rubbed on the body, the muscles relax and the parts of the body become soft and supple. By extension the word is employed for showing flexibility and softness on inappropriate occasions — and hence it is used in the sense of hypocrisy. These are people who go smooth against the truth rather than meet it.
