Ibn Kathir gives the early glosses. Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that *mudhinūn* means "you do not believe in and deny" — and ad-Dahhak, Abu Hazrah and as-Suddi said the like. Mujahid gave a different angle: "you want to fill yourselves with and rely upon."

## "And you make your provision your denial" (82)

Ayah 82 is startlingly compressed. Some of the scholars said that *rizq*, "provision," here has the meaning of *gratitude* — so the meaning is: you deny without any gratitude. ʿAli bin Abi Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited it as *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum annakum tukadhdhibūn* — "and you show your gratitude by denying."

And Ibn 'Abbas said exactly what denial he had in mind: "It has never rained upon a people except that some of them became disbelievers by saying, 'Such and such position of a star sent rain!'" Ibn Kathir notes that this chain of narration is Sahih to Ibn 'Abbas. Notice the circle closing: the sūrah swore *by the setting-places of the stars* — and the ingratitude it names is crediting rain to the position of a star.

Ibn Kathir then brings the hadith. In his Muwaṭṭaʼ, Malik reported from Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān, from ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUtbah ibn Masʿūd, from Zayd ibn Khālid al-Juhanī, who said: the Prophet ﷺ led us in the Ṣubḥ (dawn) prayer at al-Ḥudaybiyah after a rainy night. On completion of the prayer, he faced the congregation and said, "Do you know what your Lord has said?" Those present replied, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said:

> Allah has said: "During this morning some of My servants remained as true believers in Me and some became disbelievers. Whoever said that the rain was due to the blessings and the mercy of Allah, had belief in Me, and he disbelieves in the stars; and whoever said that it rained because of a particular star, had no belief in Me, but believes in that star."

Ibn Kathir states that this hadith is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Abu Dāwud and an-Nasāʼī, all using a chain of narration in which Imam Malik was included.

The same rain falls on two men. What separates them is one sentence about where it came from. That is how tightly ayah 82 binds provision to belief: your *rizq* is either a reason to thank Allah or a reason to credit something else — and the second is what "you make your provision your denial" means.

## Living it

Qatadah said that al-Hasan used to say: "How evil is that all that some people have earned for themselves from the Book of Allah, is denying it!" Ibn Kathir explains the sense — such people gained no benefit from the Book of Allah because they denied it.

Set against that, the passage asks three plain things. **Reverence the Book** — the purity the jurists require before touching a written copy of the Qur'an is a trained echo of ayah 79. **Refuse to be *mudhin*** — do not go soft and pliant before this discourse, half-agreeing to avoid the cost of agreeing. And **name the true Giver** — when the rain comes, say it came by the blessings and the mercy of Allah. That single sentence, said at dawn after a wet night, was enough to place a man on one side or the other.

passages.title: The dying soul you cannot bring back
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take the single most public, most repeated, most undeniable event in human experience — a person dying while those who love him look on — and turn it into an argument. Allah does not ask the deniers of the Hereafter for a theory. He asks them for a demonstration: the soul is at the throat, everyone is watching, now bring it back.

## What holds the passage together

Both of our commentators handle these five ayat as one continuous statement rather than five separate remarks. Ibn Kathir quotes all five together before he begins to comment, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders them as a single connected question: *So why do you not interfere when the soul of a dying person reaches the throat, and you are watching? And We are closer to him than you, but you do not perceive. So, if you are not going to be recompensed in the Hereafter for your deeds, then why do you not bring the soul back, if you are truthful?*

Ayah 83 sets the moment — when it reaches the throat. Ayah 84 sets the onlookers — while you are looking on. Ayah 85 discloses what is in that room which the onlookers cannot see. Ayah 86 states the deniers' own position back to them. And ayah 87 delivers the demand: bring that soul back, if what you say is true.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the passage in its argument. The verses before it, it explains, proved two facts through rational arguments and by swearing an oath by the falling stars: first, that the Holy Qur'an is the word of Allah — neither jinn nor devil can ever tamper with it, and everything it contains is the truth; and second, that one of the most fundamental articles of faith enshrined in the Qur'an is the Day of Resurrection and Reckoning. Then, towards the end of the passage, it is mentioned that the infidels and idolaters reject life after death in spite of clear arguments and evidence.

**The hidden claim being refuted.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts its finger on what denial of the Resurrection really implies: their denial amounts, in a way, to a claim that their lives and souls are under their own control, and that they have a say in the matter of life and death. That is the assumption these ayat are built to refute. Not by counter-argument, but by walking the denier over to a deathbed and letting him look.

## "When it reaches the throat" (ayah 83)

Ibn Kathir explains the opening plainly. *Falawlā idhā balaghat* — "Then why do you not intervene when it reaches" — is, he says, in reference to the soul; and *al-ḥulqūm* means the throat, at the time of death. The Arabic says only "when **it** reaches the throat"; Ibn Kathir tells us what "it" is.

Ibn Kathir then brings a parallel from Sūrat al-Qiyāmah to fill out the picture:

> "Nay, when the soul reaches to the collar bone, and it will be said: 'Who can cure him (and save him from death)?' And he will conclude that it was the time of parting (death); and one leg will be joined with another leg (shrouded). The drive will be on that Day to your Lord." (75:26–30)

Notice what that passage adds. *Who can cure him?* — the search for anyone who might intervene, which is exactly the helplessness ayah 84 puts on display. *He will conclude that it was the parting* — the dying man's own certainty, arriving at the end. And then the destination: the drive, that Day, is to your Lord. The soul at the throat is not going nowhere. It is going somewhere, and the ayat before us are asking whether you can stop it.

**"And you at that moment are looking on" (ayah 84).** Ibn Kathir glosses this as looking at the dying person and witnessing the stupor of death that he is experiencing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the human scene: when the soul reaches his throat, all of his near and dear ones look at him and express their desire that he may live longer, but none of them is able to intervene and save his life; all the people around him seem absolutely helpless. Everything that human love and human power can supply is present in that room — and it changes nothing. The two commentators meet exactly here: what those present do is look; what they cannot do is intervene.

## "We are nearer to him than you" (ayah 85)

This is the heart of the passage, and our two sources approach it from different angles.

**Ibn Kathir** reads the nearness in connection with Allah's angels: "But We are nearer to him than you" — with Our angels; "but you see not" — you cannot see the angels. On this reading the ayah is disclosing what is actually in the room. The family can see the body, the laboured breathing, the fading eyes. They cannot see the angels. Ibn Kathir supports this with another ayah:

> "He is the Irresistible over His servants, and He sends guardians (angels) over you, until when death approaches one of you, Our messengers take his soul, and they never neglect their duty. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Protector. Surely, for Him is the judgement and He is the swiftest in taking account." (6:61–62)

Every clause there does work in our passage. *They never neglect their duty* — the taking of the soul is not careless or haphazard. *Then they are returned to Allah, their true Protector* — the moment the onlookers experience as an ending is, from the other side, a return. And *for Him is the judgement, and He is the swiftest in taking account* — which is precisely the reckoning that ayah 86 will raise.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** explains the nearness in terms of knowledge and power: Allah is nearer to the dying person than the people around him even though they are unable to see Him — nearer, that is, in terms of knowledge and power. He is fully aware of the person's inner and outer conditions and has complete control over him. Maʿārif states it once more, even more strongly: Allah is nearer to a dying person than his own soul or life.

Both commentators, then, leave the ayah standing as it is and tell us what it means for the dying man: unseen messengers of Allah are present, and nothing about him is hidden from Allah or beyond Allah's power. As for the closing clause, Ibn Kathir's gloss is simply "you cannot see the angels" — what is happening at that bedside is not exhausted by what the people in the room can see.

## "If you are not to be recompensed" (ayah 86)

Everything now turns on one word: *madīnīn* (مَدِينِينَ). Ibn Kathir renders the sense of ayat 86–87 as: *Will you not return this soul, that has reached the throat, to its body as it used to be, if you are exempt from the reckoning and recompense?*

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites unpack the word:

- **Saʿīd bin Jubayr and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī:** "If you do not believe that you will be reckoned, recompensed, resurrected and punished, then why do you not return this soul to its body?"
- **Mujāhid:** *ghayra madīnīn* means "if you are not certain."

Both readings press on the same nerve. On the first, *madīnīn* concerns the whole complex of accountability — being reckoned, recompensed, resurrected, punished. On the second, it is the denier's *own certainty* that is under examination: you speak as though you were sure. Are you? The rendering in the translation before us — "if you are not subject to Our Will as you claim" — carries the same force as the claim Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identified: to deny the Reckoning is to speak as though your life and soul were under your own control.

## "Bring that soul back, if you are truthful" (ayah 87)

The demand of ayah 87 is not rhetorical cruelty. It is the fairest possible test of the claim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the logic: in view of this graphic picture, the disbelievers are reminded that if they think they cannot be resurrected after death, and that they are too strong to come under Allah's grasp, then they must restore the soul when it has reached the throat and is about to depart from the body — or after it has already departed and the person has died. If it is not possible to do any of these, Maʿārif asks, how illogical and irrational it is for man to think that he can escape the Divine grasp and reject life after death.

Put the argument in a line: **you cannot keep the life you already have going a moment longer than its time; on what basis do you announce what Allah can and cannot do with you afterwards?**

Ibn Kathir heads this passage with the conclusion it is driving at: when the soul reaches the throat at the time of death it cannot be brought back — and this proves that the Reckoning shall occur. The inference runs from the observed to the unseen. Your helplessness at the deathbed is evidence, presented daily and in public, that life and death are not in your hands.

## Living with these ayat

The passage was revealed against deniers, but it does not leave the believer untouched.

**The appointed time is fixed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it directly: Allah has pre-designated a particular time for the soul to be separated from the body, and none can avert it. Whatever else that means for how we live, it means the timing of that moment was never ours to negotiate — which can turn panic into trust, and turn the sickbed into a place of duʿāʾ rather than a place of bargaining.

**Nothing you love can save you, and you cannot save what you love.** Ayah 84 is a portrait of exactly the people who would give anything to help — and cannot. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the conclusion bluntly: it is simply not within people's power to get together and save a soul or a life. Take that seriously now, while there is still time to act.

**You are never alone, and never unobserved.** Whatever else is true of the dying man in ayah 85, this is true: Allah is nearer to him than the family holding his hand — nearer in knowledge and in power, fully aware of his inner and outer condition. For the one who has lived in denial, that is the closing of every escape route. For the believer, it is the deepest comfort the passage offers — that at the moment when every human being in the room becomes helpless, the One who is nearer than all of them is the One you have been calling on all along.

**And the seen is not the whole of the real.** "But you do not perceive." On Ibn Kathir's reading, the angels are in that room and no one present can see them; and the Reckoning, which Mujāhid says the deniers are not certain of, is coming regardless. A faith built only on what the eye can verify would have missed the most important thing happening at that bedside — and will miss the most important thing about your own.

passages.title: Three destinies at death, and the sūrah's seal
passages.tafsir:
The sūrah that opened by sorting all humanity into three groups now closes by putting each of us on our own deathbed and asking which group we die in. Ayat 88–94 give three conditions a person can be in at the moment the soul leaves; ayah 95 seals them as certain; ayah 96 tells the Prophet ﷺ — and through him every believer — what to do with that certainty.

## The sūrah folds back on itself

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the thread. The preceding verses had made clear that one day the present world will come to an end; that at the time of death the near and dear ones, friends and relatives, and doctors all stand helplessly around the dying person; and that resurrection, reckoning, and reward and punishment after the account of deeds are all a reality and a certainty of the highest degree. And at the very beginning of the sūrah, it was mentioned that there will be three categories of people in regard to their reward or punishment. Now, says Maʿārif, "the gist of this subject is again summarized here." The sūrah ends where it began, but with the scene narrowed from the cosmic to the intimate — from the end of the world to one bed, one breath, one person.

Ibn Kathir titles this section simply: **the condition of people at the time of their death.** "These are the three types of conditions that people face upon their death." Either they are among the near believers, or those below their rank on the right, or those who denied the truth, were led astray from the guidance and were ignorant about Allah. Three conditions — and no fourth is named.

## Whose condition is being described

The ayah says only فَأَمَّآ إِن كَانَ — "Then if he be…". Ibn Kathir supplies the subject for us: "(Then if he), in reference to the dying person." Maʿārif does the same, glossing the verse as "So, in case he [the dying person] is from among those blessed with nearness."

So this is not a passage about nations or eras. It is about one person at one moment — and each of the three cases is stated as a condition, "if he be", rather than as an announcement about any named individual.

## The first door: rawḥ and rayḥān (88–89)

**Who are the muqarrabūn?** Ibn Kathir defines "those brought near" with real precision: those "who fulfilled the obligations and the recommended acts of worship and avoided the forbidden and disliked matters and even some of the allowed." Read that slowly. The obligatory is the floor of his description, not the ceiling. What he describes is a person who does more than is required and leaves more than is forbidden — declining even some permitted things.

**What they receive.** فَرَوۡحٞ وَرَيۡحَانٞ وَجَنَّتُ نَعِيمٖ — *rawḥ*, *rayḥān*, and a Garden of Delights. Ibn Kathir gathers what the early authorities said about these two words:

- ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: **rawḥ** means rest, and **rayḥān** means the place of rest.
- Mujāhid said similarly that rawḥ means rest. Abū Ḥazrah said rawḥ means "rest from the world."
- Saʿīd bin Jubayr and As-Suddī said it means to rejoice.
- And from Mujāhid: rawḥ and rayḥān mean "Paradise and delights."
- Qatādah said that rawḥ means mercy.
- Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr said that rayḥān means provisions.

Then Ibn Kathir does something worth learning from. He does not pick a winner. He says: "All of these explanations are correct and similar in meaning. The near believers who die will earn all of these; mercy, rest, provision, joy, happiness and good delights."

**When does it arrive?** Not after the Judgement — at the deathbed. Ibn Kathir says the glad tidings of these traits "will be conveyed to them by the angels at the time of death," and he recalls the Prophet's ﷺ ḥadīth narrated from al-Barāʾ in which the angels of mercy say to a dying, believing person:

> "O good soul in the good body that you inhabited, come to Rawh, Rayhan and a Lord Who is not angry."

Notice the form of the words the angels use: not a summons, but an invitation — *come to*.

Abū al-ʿĀliyah added a striking detail: "None of the near believers will depart (this life) until after he is brought a branch of the Rayhan of Paradise and his soul is captured in it." And Muḥammad bin Kaʿb said, "Every person who dies will know upon his death if he is among the people of Paradise or the people of the Fire." Whatever uncertainty a person carries through life, it ends there.

Ibn Kathir also cites what is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the souls of the martyrs live in the bodies of green birds, flying wherever they wish in the Gardens of Paradise, and then rest in chandeliers hung from the Throne.

## The narration that reframes the whole passage

Ibn Kathir tells this with its scene intact, and the scene is half the point. Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAṭāʾ bin as-Sāʾib said: "The first day I saw ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Abī Laylā, I saw an old man whose hair had become white on his head and beard. He was riding his donkey and following a funeral. I heard him say, 'So-and-so narrated to me that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say,

> "He who likes to meet Allah, Allah likes to meet him, and he who hates to meet Allah, Allah hates to meet him."

Note the chain exactly as Ibn Kathir gives it: the old man does not say he heard this from the Prophet ﷺ himself. He says "So-and-so narrated to me that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say" — there is an unnamed narrator standing between them, and the text preserves that gap rather than filling it.

The narration continues: the people around him started weeping, and he asked them why they wept. They said: **"All of us hate death."**

That is one of the most human sentences in the whole passage. These are believers, and they are honest: nobody wants to die. And the answer given, as the narration continues, was: *"It does not mean that. When one dies…"* — and then these very ayat. If he be of the near believers, then rawḥ, rayḥān and a Garden of Delights — **and when this good news is conveyed to him, he likes to meet Allah, and Allah likes, even more, to meet him.** But if he be of the denying, the erring, then an entertainment with ḥamīm and entry in Hellfire — and when that news is conveyed to him, he hates to meet Allah, and Allah hates, even more, to meet him.

So what is being measured is not your feelings about death today, in good health, over breakfast. It is the instant of disclosure, when each soul is given the news and reacts. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the narration Imam Ahmad collected, and that in the Ṣaḥīḥ there is a ḥadīth with this meaning collected from ʿĀʾishah.

(On creed: Allah's love and His hatred are attributes we affirm exactly as He and His Messenger ﷺ described them, without likening them to the loves and hatreds of creation, and without emptying the words of their meaning.)

## The second door: "Peace be to you" (90–91)

For those on the right — *aṣḥāb al-yamīn*, whom Maʿārif identifies as "the general body of believers," those who are "not from the Foremost" yet who "will also experience the bounties and pleasures of Paradise" — the answer in ayah 91 is not a list of gifts at all. It is a sentence spoken to a person: فَسَلَٰمٞ لَّكَ — "then peace be to you."

Someone must be speaking those words. Ibn Kathir explains: the angels will deliver the good news to them by saying, "Peace be upon you" — that is, "be calm, you will be led to safety, you are among those on the right." He quotes ʿIkrimah: "The angels will greet him with the Salam and convey to him the news that he is among those on the right." Ibn Kathir calls this "a good explanation," and says it conforms with Allah's statement elsewhere: those who say "Our Lord is Allah" and then stand firm, upon whom the angels descend saying, *"Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you have been promised! We have been your friends in the life of this world and are (so) in the Hereafter…"* (41:30–32).

There is enormous comfort in this. The ordinary believer — not among the *muqarrabūn*, carrying a lifetime of ordinary failures — is met at the hardest moment of his existence with a greeting and the words *be calm*.

## The third door: an entertainment with ḥamīm (92–94)

وَأَمَّآ إِن كَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُكَذِّبِينَ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ — "But if he be of the denying, the erring." Ibn Kathir glosses: if the dying person "is one of those who denied the truth, who were led astray from guidance" — and, in his opening summary, those who "were ignorant about Allah." Maʿārif calls them the People of the Left hand, "the deniers and the deviant ones."

Then comes one of the Qurʾān's most cutting word choices. فَنُزُلٞ مِّنۡ حَمِيمٖ — rendered "then for him is an entertainment," which Ibn Kathir spells out: "meaning, as a guest." The same word stands in the passage he quotes from Sūrah Fuṣṣilat, where Paradise is *nuzulan min ghafūrin raḥīm*, "an entertainment from the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Both are receptions; both are what the host has laid on for the arriving guest. The difference is what is served: here, *ḥamīm* — scalding water which, Ibn Kathir says, "dissolves his intestines and skin." And in ayah 94, وَتَصۡلِيَةُ جَحِيمٍ, entry in Hellfire: "he will reside in Hellfire, which will engulf him from every direction."

Maʿārif states the third case plainly: if he is one of the People of the Left hand, "then he will be in the blazing fire of Hell where he will be served with boiling water to drink."

## The seal of certainty (95)

إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَهُوَ حَقُّ ٱلۡيَقِينِ — "Verily, this! This is an absolute truth with certainty," in Ibn Kathir's rendering; "Indeed this is certainty in its true sense," in Maʿārif's. Ibn Kathir's gloss has two halves: "this news is the truth; there is no doubt about it, nor escape from it for anyone." Maʿārif says none of the reward or punishment mentioned in the preceding verses is refutable, "because they are a dead certainty that has no room for any doubt or suspicion."

Hold on to Ibn Kathir's two halves. First, it is *true* — the report is accurate. Second, there is **no escape from it for anyone** — the sorting will happen to you whether or not you accept the report. That second clause turns the passage from information into urgency.

## And therefore: glorify (96)

فَسَبِّحۡ بِٱسۡمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلۡعَظِيمِ. Both renderings in front of us begin the same way — "**So**, glorify with praises the Name of your Lord, the Most Great" (Ibn Kathir), "**So**, proclaim the purity of the name of your Lord, the Magnificent" (Maʿārif). The command is presented as the conclusion drawn from everything before it. Given the three doors, given that the news admits no doubt and no escape — glorify the name of your Lord. The response the sūrah asks for is not panic. It is *tasbīḥ*: proclaiming the purity of your Lord's name, declaring Him free of every deficiency, joined to His praise.

Maʿārif notes that this closing imperative is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that it "includes all kinds of tasbihat (rememberances) — within salah and outside salah. Salah itself is sometimes referred to as tasbih. Thus this verse enjoins to keep up the regular performance of salah." So the sūrah that spent ninety-five ayat on the end of the world lands on a daily habit: pray, and keep your tongue busy with the greatness of Allah.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on the whole sūrah with two narrations about exactly that:

- Jābir narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"He who says, 'Glory be to Allah the Magnificent and with His praise!' — then a date tree will be planted for him in Paradise."* This ḥadīth was collected by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī; at-Tirmidhī said, "Hasan Gharib."
- Al-Bukhārī recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Two statements that are light on the tongue, but heavy on the Balance, and most beloved to ar-Raḥmān: 'Glory be to Allah and with His praise, glory be to Allah the Magnificent.'"* The Group, with the exception of Abū Dāwūd, collected this.

The name in ayah 96 is *al-ʿAẓīm*, the Magnificent — and both narrations put that same word onto your tongue. The sūrah hands you the phrase it ends with.

## Living it

**Aim above the minimum.** Ibn Kathir's description of the *muqarrabūn* reads like a ladder rather than a label: obligations fulfilled, recommended acts added, the forbidden avoided, the disliked avoided, and even some of the allowed let go. Every rung is available to an ordinary person today.

**Do not measure yourself by your dread of dying.** The people in that narration said openly, "All of us hate death," and the answer was not a rebuke but a correction: "It does not mean that. When one dies…" What is described is the moment of disclosure, not your feelings in health. The work is to build a life whose disclosure you would welcome.

**Take the "So" seriously.** The passage's own conclusion from all this news is two short statements you can say while walking — light on the tongue, heavy on the Balance — and a ṣalāh you do not abandon. Certainty about the Hereafter is meant to come out of the mouth and into the limbs, not to sit in the head as information.
